orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the February 29, 2012 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted summary judgment dismissing complaint against Hariri and Jen-Kev.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on an ice patch in the shopping-center parking lot owned by Hariri and managed by Jen-Kev. He attributed it to piled snow melting and refreezing, a theory the court found speculative.

legal_issues.finding: Owner and manager established noncreation prima facie; opposition raised no issue. Piled-snow melt/refreeze theory was speculative.
Owner and manager established lack of actual notice prima facie; opposition raised no issue. Piled-snow melt/refreeze theory was speculative.
Owner and manager established lack of constructive notice prima facie; opposition raised no issue. Piled-snow melt/refreeze theory was speculative.

quality.notes: Explicit private ownership. No evidence formats, accident date, customer role or storm-in-progress finding supplied. General nondelegable-duty standard is not a separate disputed duty ruling.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff alleged that he slipped and fell on a patch of ice in a parking lot of a shopping center owned by the defendant Hariri Realty Associates, Inc. (hereinafter Hariri), and managed by the defendant Jen-Kev Management, LLC (hereinafter Jen-Kev).

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Mahon, J), dated February 29, 2012, which granted the motion of the defendants Hariri Realty Associates, Inc., and Jen-Kev Management, LLC, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them.

Hariri and Jen-Kev established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that they neither created nor had actual or constructive notice of the icy condition alleged to have caused the plaintiffs fall. The plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact in opposition
The plaintiffs theory that the ice resulted from piled snow that melted and then re-froze was speculative and, thus, insufficient to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the motion of Hariri and Jen-Kev for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them.

orders.description: Defendant’s limited appeal from the September 22, 2023 order.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on rainwater on an interior staircase in defendant’s building leased to her employer. She claimed water entered beneath a defective exterior door; lease and representative evidence assigned door maintenance to the tenant.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant negated the relevant contractual maintenance duty; plaintiff raised no triable issue.
Defendant established out-of-possession status without a contractual duty to maintain the door; tenant responsibility was supported by lease and representative evidence.
Plaintiff’s Property Maintenance Code theory was unpleaded and improperly introduced in opposition; code applicability/violation was not decided.
New code-violation theory was not pleaded in complaint or bill of particulars and could not defeat the motion.

evidence_discussed.description: Lease copy and evidence from landlord/tenant representatives established tenant door-maintenance responsibility; representative evidence format unspecified.

quality.notes: Express ownership/lease support private premises; church identity does not specify actual building use, so premises_type unclear. Tenant employer is not listed as a defendant. No accident date, proven door defect or independent statutory duty inferred. Unchanged rules for 2024 opinion.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.

The plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on rainwater in an interior staircase of a building owned by the defendant and leased to the plaintiff's employer. The plaintiff claimed that the rainwater had seeped into the building under a defective exterior door.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Diccia T. Pineda-Kirwan, J.), dated September 22, 2023. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Insofar as relevant here, the defendant demonstrated, prima facie, that it was an out-of-possession landlord which did not have a contractual duty to maintain the door at issue

In support of its motion, the defendant submitted, inter alia, a copy of the lease agreement and evidence from its representatives and the tenant's representative, which demonstrated that the tenant was responsible [*2] for maintaining the door.

In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. The plaintiff improperly asserted a new theory of liability based on violations of the New York State Property Maintenance Code, which was not pleaded in her complaint or bill of particulars
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s limited appeal from the November 29, 2016 order.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff fell from an exterior staircase on defendant’s property in Westchester on August 6, 2013. The physical mechanism and alleged hazard are unstated.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant’s submissions, including plaintiff’s deposition and surveillance, established inability to identify cause; plaintiff raised no triable issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted plaintiff’s deposition transcripts supporting inability to identify cause.
Defendant submitted footage of the fall; the opinion does not describe visible mechanics.

quality.notes: Review private-property support and incident scope: defendant’s property alone gives no title/use/control basis, and fell from stairs does not specify a slip/trip. No hazard, injured role or corporate ownership inferred. Inability to identify negligent cause alone is not an exclusion; uncertainty concerns source support for private status and mechanism. Third-party caption is ancillary.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.
On August 6, 2013, the plaintiff fell from an exterior staircase on the defendant's property in Westchester.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (Terry Jane Ruderman, J.), dated November 29, 2016. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted that branch of the defendant's cross motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the evidence submitted by the defendant in support of its cross motion, including the deposition transcripts of the plaintiff and surveillance footage of the plaintiff's fall, was sufficient to establish, prima facie, that the plaintiff did not know what had caused her to fall
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted that branch of the defendant's cross motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the March 16, 2023 order.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on water in a residential laundry room, claiming leakage from a washer she used. She saw no water about 40 minutes earlier; vendor evidence described a working machine after service three days earlier and on the accident day, with excess soap causing any leak.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants established noncreation and reasonable safety through plaintiff’s account and vendor evidence. Daughter’s affidavit showed general awareness, not actual knowledge of a recurring hazard sufficient to defeat the showing.

Defendants established lack of actual notice and reasonable safety through plaintiff’s account and vendor evidence. Daughter’s affidavit showed general awareness, not actual knowledge of a recurring hazard sufficient to defeat the showing.

Defendants established lack of constructive notice and reasonable safety through plaintiff’s account and vendor evidence. Daughter’s affidavit showed general awareness, not actual knowledge of a recurring hazard sufficient to defeat the showing.
Daughter’s affidavit showed only general awareness of occasional leaks; plaintiff failed to raise an issue of actual notice of a recurring hazardous condition imputing constructive notice.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition described no water about 40 minutes earlier.
Plaintiff’s daughter’s opposition affidavit described occasional leaks, insufficient to establish recurring-condition notice.
Vendor service/inspection evidence reported working condition and excess-soap explanation; precise evidentiary format unspecified.

quality.notes: Private residential ownership/management explicit; no tenancy inferred merely from laundry use. Excess-soap finding is vendor evidence, not an express plaintiff-fault allocation. No maintenance record format, accident date or expert status assigned to vendor. Opinion date 2024 controls despite 2025 correction metadata; unchanged rules.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.

The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on water in the laundry room of a residential building owned and managed by the defendants. The plaintiff alleged that water was leaking from a washing machine that she was using.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Robin S. Garson, J.), dated March 16, 2023. The order denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendants established, prima facie, that they maintained their premises in a reasonably safe condition and that they did not create the alleged hazardous condition or have actual or constructive notice of its existence

In support of their motion, the defendants submitted, inter alia, a transcript of the deposition testimony of the plaintiff, who testified that she did not see any water when she was last in the laundry room approximately 40 minutes prior to the accident. The defendants also submitted evidence that the machine was serviced by a vendor three days prior to the incident and that when the vendor left the premises, the machine was in working condition. When the vendor inspected the machine again on the day of the accident, the vendor determined that the machine was in working condition and that any leak was caused by the use of too much soap.

In opposition, the [*2] plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether the defendants had actual notice of a recurring hazardous condition and, thus, could be charged with constructive notice of the subject condition. The plaintiff's daughter's affidavit submitted in opposition to the motion merely showed that the defendants had a general awareness that, at times, water leaked from the machine at issue
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the September 16, 2014 order.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on accumulated snow and ice in defendant’s parking lot around 7:30 a.m. on January 7, 2009. The dispute was whether the fall involved old accumulation from a prior storm rather than current precipitation.

legal_issues.finding: Plaintiffs raised a triable issue of constructive notice of the old snow/ice; neither duration nor notice was conclusively adjudicated.
Ongoing storm established and undisputed, but opposing evidence raised issues about a causal preexisting condition and constructive notice.
Plaintiffs’ meteorologist report was included in defendant’s storm showing and plaintiffs’ preexisting-condition opposition; the court found the overall submissions sufficient to raise an issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiffs’ meteorologist report was submitted on both sides of the motion.
Certified climatological data supported both the storm showing and opposition concerning prior accumulation.
Defendant submitted parties’ deposition transcripts; injured plaintiff also supplied an opposition affidavit.
Two nonparty witness affidavits were included in opposition concerning old accumulation and notice.

quality.notes: Explicit private lot ownership. Do not attribute plaintiffs’ expert to defendant merely because defendant submitted the report. Actual notice appears in general standard, but specific opposition holding is constructive notice. No date of prior storm, evidence measurements, role or negligent removal method inferred.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff Thomas Burniston (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) alleged that on January 7, 2009, at approximately 7:30 a.m., he slipped and fell due to an accumulation of snow and ice in a parking lot owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Putnam County (Lubell, J.), dated September 16, 2014, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The evidence submitted by the defendant in support of its motion for summary judgment, including certified climatological data, a report from the plaintiffs' own expert meteorologist, and the transcripts of the deposition testimony of the parties, demonstrated, prima facie, that a storm was in progress at the time of the subject accident

The plaintiffs raised a triable issue of fact in this regard. The evidence relied upon by the plaintiffs in opposition to the defendant's motion, which included the report of their expert meteorologist, certified climatological data, and the affidavits of the injured plaintiff and two nonparty witnesses, raised a triable issue of fact as to whether the injured plaintiff slipped and fell on old snow and ice that was the product of a prior storm, as opposed to precipitation from the storm in progress, and as to whether the defendant had constructive notice of the preexisting condition
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment.
